stem: A team built a document-processing system as a fixed sequence of predefined code paths: extract, validate, format, deliver — each step's logic is hard-coded and the same steps run every time regardless of document content. A stakeholder calls this "an agent." What's the more accurate architectural label, and why does the distinction matter?
explanation: A system following predefined code paths with no model-driven control over what happens next is a workflow, not an agent — an agent dynamically directs its own process and tool use based on what it encounters. The distinction matters because it drives which failure modes and design considerations apply: workflows are predictable and easy to reason about but inflexible; agents adapt but are harder to bound and verify.

choices.text: It's a workflow — hard-coded steps with no model-driven control over what happens next
choices.reasoning: Correct: the defining line is whether the model dynamically directs the process (agent) or the code path is fixed in advance (workflow) — this system is clearly the latter, and the label matters for reasoning about its failure modes and guarantees.

choices.text: It's an agent, because it processes documents using Claude at each step
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: using Claude for a step's content processing doesn't make the overall system an agent if the sequence and branching logic itself is fixed and hard-coded rather than dynamically decided.

choices.text: The distinction is purely marketing terminology with no architectural consequence
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the workflow/agent distinction has real consequences for predictability, testability, and where dynamic judgment is exercised — it's not a cosmetic label.

choices.text: It's an agent, because it has more than one step in its pipeline
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: step count doesn't determine the label; a multi-step pipeline with fully predetermined, non-adaptive logic is still a workflow.

choices.text: It's a workflow only if it uses the Batch API, and an agent otherwise
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: batch versus real-time is an unrelated processing-mode choice; the workflow/agent distinction is about whether the model dynamically controls the process.

choices.text: Neither label applies unless the system uses more than one subagent
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a single-agent system can still be a genuine agent if it dynamically directs its own actions; subagent count isn't what defines the workflow/agent distinction.

stem: A coding agent is about to run a Bash command that would delete an entire test fixtures directory as part of a "cleanup" step it decided on its own. The team wants a chance to block genuinely destructive commands before they execute, not just log them afterward. Which hook type fits, and why not the alternative?
explanation: A PreToolUse hook intercepts before the tool call executes, letting the application inspect and block it outright — the only point in the loop where a destructive action can be prevented rather than merely observed. A PostToolUse hook runs after execution, which is too late to stop the deletion itself.

choices.text: PreToolUse — it intercepts before execution and can block the command outright
choices.reasoning: Correct: only a hook that runs before execution can prevent a destructive command from ever running; PostToolUse observes and can transform output, but by then the deletion is already done.

choices.text: PostToolUse — it can undo a destructive command after the fact, which is equally effective
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: undoing a directory deletion after the fact isn't guaranteed to be possible, and PostToolUse's documented role is inspecting/transforming completed output, not reversing already-executed destructive actions.

choices.text: Either works equally well; the choice between PreToolUse and PostToolUse doesn't matter for blocking behavior
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: only PreToolUse runs before execution — the timing difference is exactly what determines whether a destructive action can be blocked versus merely observed after it already happened.

choices.text: Neither hook type can block a Bash tool call; only permissions.deny rules can
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: PreToolUse hooks are explicitly documented as able to block tool calls programmatically, including Bash calls.

choices.text: PostToolUse, since it's the only hook type that has access to the command's arguments
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: PreToolUse also has access to the pending call's arguments before it executes — that's precisely what lets it decide whether to block it.

choices.text: PreToolUse, but only because it's cheaper in tokens than PostToolUse
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the reason to prefer PreToolUse here is the ability to block before execution, not a token-cost difference between the two hook types.

stem: A coordinator dispatches four subagents to independently verify four different clauses of a contract for compliance risk. Three return `{"clause": str, "risk_level": str, "citation": str}`; the fourth, built later by a different engineer, returns `{"finding": str, "severity": int, "source_paragraph": str}` — a different field naming and typing scheme entirely. What breaks as a result, and what's the fix?
explanation: Parallel execution requires a uniform output shape across subagents so the coordinator can synthesize results generically; a mismatched shape forces special-case handling for that one subagent and undermines automated synthesis across all four. The fix is standardizing every subagent's output to the same field names and types.

choices.text: The mismatched field names break generic synthesis; standardize all four subagents' output shape
choices.reasoning: Correct: uniform output shape is what lets the coordinator process results generically — a mismatched shape from even one subagent forces special-case handling, which the fix eliminates by standardizing field names and types across all four.

choices.text: Nothing breaks; the coordinator can always synthesize results regardless of field naming differences
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: differing field names and types (risk_level vs. severity, string vs. int) require the coordinator to special-case the fourth subagent's output rather than processing all four uniformly.

choices.text: The fix is to drop the fourth subagent's findings entirely rather than reconcile the schema
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: discarding a legitimate compliance-risk finding over a naming mismatch wastes real analysis; standardizing the shape is the appropriate fix, not discarding the content.

choices.text: The fix is to switch all four subagents to the Batch API, which automatically normalizes output shape
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: batch processing doesn't normalize or standardize response content shape; that's a schema/prompt design decision, independent of which API mode is used.

choices.text: The fix is to merge all four subagents into a single subagent so shape mismatches can't occur
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: merging discards the benefit of independent parallel verification; the actual fix is standardizing each subagent's output shape, not eliminating parallelism.

choices.text: The fix is to give the fourth subagent a higher-tier model so its output is more accurate
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: model tier affects accuracy of content, not the structural field-naming mismatch that's actually breaking synthesis here.

stem: An agent generating a long report hits its configured max_tokens mid-sentence, and the response comes back with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` instead of `end_turn` or `tool_use`. The loop-control code currently only branches on whether stop_reason equals `"tool_use"`, treating anything else as "done." What's wrong with that handling here?
explanation: `max_tokens` indicates the response was truncated due to the output length limit, not that Claude is actually finished — treating it identically to `end_turn` causes the loop to stop while the response is incomplete. The correct handling distinguishes truncation (which may need a continuation request or a raised limit) from genuine completion.

choices.text: Treating max_tokens the same as end_turn stops the loop on a truncated, incomplete response
choices.reasoning: Correct: max_tokens and end_turn mean very different things — one is an incomplete cutoff, the other is genuine completion — and collapsing them into the same "stop" branch silently ships truncated output as if it were finished.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong; max_tokens and end_turn should always be handled identically since both are not tool_use
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is exactly the flaw being asked about — max_tokens signals truncation, a materially different situation from a genuinely completed end_turn response.

choices.text: The fix is to always increase max_tokens to an arbitrarily large value so this never happens
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this doesn't address handling the stop_reason correctly when truncation does occur for other reasons (e.g. a genuinely very long report), and doesn't fix the loop's underlying logic gap.

choices.text: The fix is to parse the truncated text to guess where the sentence would have ended
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this reintroduces exactly the kind of unreliable text-parsing heuristic the loop should avoid, instead of branching on the structured stop_reason value itself.

choices.text: This is only a problem if the report is being generated via the Batch API
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: max_tokens truncation and its stop_reason value apply the same way regardless of whether the request went through the Batch or real-time API.

choices.text: This is only a problem if tool calls are involved in the same conversation
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the max_tokens/end_turn confusion applies even in a conversation with no tool calls at all — it's about correctly distinguishing truncation from completion generally.

stem: A CI pipeline runs a full coordinator-plus-three-parallel-subagent architecture just to check whether a single config file's version number was bumped before merge — a check a single grep-and-compare tool call could answer directly. Builds now take noticeably longer for this trivial check. What should the architect change?
explanation: Running a full multi-agent pipeline for a simple, directly-answerable check is a documented anti-pattern — orchestration overhead should be proportional to the complexity of the work. A single tool call (or the coordinator answering directly) is sufficient here; the fuller pipeline should be reserved for genuinely complex checks.

choices.text: Replace the full pipeline with a single direct tool call for this simple version-bump check
choices.reasoning: Correct: this directly fixes the reported slowdown by scaling orchestration overhead to actual task complexity instead of applying a heavy pipeline to a trivial, single-fact check.

choices.text: Add a fourth parallel subagent so the check completes faster through more parallelism
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: adding more subagents to an already-unnecessary pipeline for a trivial check increases overhead rather than reducing the reported build-time slowdown.

choices.text: Switch the pipeline to the Batch API to reduce cost
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: Batch has no SLA and unpredictable turnaround, unsuitable for a CI check that gates a merge and needs a prompt result — this would make the pipeline slower and less reliable, not fix the reported slowdown.

choices.text: Keep the pipeline as-is; multi-agent architectures are inherently more thorough regardless of task complexity
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: thoroughness isn't needed for a single deterministic version-number comparison — this is exactly the over-engineering trap the guidance warns against.

choices.text: Give each subagent a broader toolset so the check resolves faster
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a broader toolset per subagent doesn't address the core issue — the full pipeline shouldn't be invoked at all for a simple, directly-answerable comparison.

choices.text: Move the check to a higher-tier model within the same three-subagent pipeline
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: upgrading model tier within an unnecessarily heavy pipeline still runs the full multi-agent overhead for a check that didn't need any of it.
